source_metadata.title: DocMemo: Dynamic Evidence Discovery via Probabilistic Memory-Guided Retrieval for Multi-Modal Document Understanding
source_metadata.input_file: DocMemo Dynamic Evidence Discovery via Probabilistic Memory-Guided Retrieval for Multi-Modal Document Understanding - 2608.07067v1.pdf

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: The study proposes DocMemo to treat long-document visual question answering as dynamic evidence exploration with persistent cross-round retrieval state.
DocMemo maintains a tri-level memory state comprising Document Schema Memory, Page Belief Memory, and Question Episodic Memory.
Document Schema Memory is constructed offline from page summaries into a document type/topic description, a page-range structural index, and a global summary that remain fixed during inference.
Page Belief Memory models each page relevance as a Beta distribution whose parameters accumulate support for relevance and irrelevance.
Page Belief priors are initialized from normalized ColQwen2.5 visual relevance scores using alpha_i = S*c_i + 1 and beta_i = S*(1-c_i) + 1.
Question Episodic Memory stores per-round evidence summaries, gap analyses, and refined queries within a single question-answering session.
After each reasoning round, useful pages increment the corresponding Beta alpha parameter and irrelevant pages increment beta; unlabeled pages remain neutral.
Positive feedback is propagated to neighboring pages within radius r using distance-decayed increments gamma^|j-i|, while negative feedback is not propagated.
At each round, DocMemo samples page relevance from the Beta posterior and combines the sample with current-query visual similarity using score_i=(1-lambda_t)c_i+lambda_t*theta_i.
Candidate pages are reranked by a language model using page summaries together with schema and episodic memory, then merged into a cross-round accumulated page set that can be revisited.

The reasoner terminates with an answer or not_answerable when appropriate; otherwise it produces a refined query and note that are written to episodic memory and provides useful/irrelevant page feedback for the next belief update.
Adaptive-granularity evidence access supplements full-page evidence with high-resolution local regions for information-dense pages, especially tables.
MMLongBench-Doc contains 1,082 questions over 135 long documents; documents span up to 112 pages and average 47.5 pages.
LongDocURL contains 2,325 question-answer pairs over 396 PDF documents.
PaperTab contains 393 questions over 307 scientific papers and focuses on retrieval and reasoning over tabular information.
Accuracy is the primary evaluation metric; GPT-4.1 acts as an automatic binary judge and accuracy is the proportion of predictions scored correct.
Evidence Recall is defined as the proportion of ground-truth evidence pages covered by the accumulated retrieved pages.

outcome.definition: Ground-truth evidence pages covered by accumulated retrieved pages.

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: All-Hit Rate is defined as the fraction of questions for which all annotated evidence pages are retrieved.

outcome.definition: Fraction of questions with all annotated evidence pages retrieved.

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: The main experiments use Qwen3.5-9B as the backbone, ColQwen2.5-v0.2 for visual page retrieval, vLLM for serving, and MinerU for structure-aware table and figure crops on NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
Default Page Belief settings are S=5.0, lambda=[0.0,0.3,0.6,0.6], propagation radius r=2, and decay factor gamma=0.5.
Iterative retrieval uses at most 3 retrieval-reasoning cycles, a 30-page candidate pool, at most 13 LLM-selected pages, and at most 9 pages per reasoning VLM call.
DocMemo achieved 71.3% accuracy on MMLongBench-Doc.
DocMemo achieved 81.1% accuracy on LongDocURL.
DocMemo achieved 80.4% accuracy on PaperTab.
Relative to the strongest agentic baselines identified by the authors, DocMemo improved accuracy by 3.7 percentage points on MMLongBench-Doc.
Relative to the strongest agentic baselines identified by the authors, DocMemo improved accuracy by 8.8 percentage points on LongDocURL.
Relative to the strongest agentic baselines identified by the authors, DocMemo improved accuracy by 15.0 percentage points on PaperTab.
With Qwen3-VL-8B, ColQwen2.5, and three iterative rounds held constant, DocMemo scored 61.7% versus 60.1% for SimpleDoc on MMLongBench-Doc.
With Qwen3.5-9B, ColQwen2.5, and three iterative rounds held constant, DocMemo scored 71.3% versus 69.3% for SimpleDoc on MMLongBench-Doc.
On MMLongBench-Doc table questions, DocMemo achieved 73.3% accuracy.
On MMLongBench-Doc unanswerable questions, DocMemo achieved 78.8% accuracy.
Removing all memory modules reduced MMLongBench-Doc overall accuracy from 71.28% to 68.47%.
Removing Bayesian updating reduced MMLongBench-Doc overall accuracy from 71.28% to 68.80%.
Removing adaptive-granularity evidence access reduced MMLongBench-Doc table-question accuracy from 73.27% to 68.66%.
Replacing Thompson sampling with greedy posterior-mean selection reduced MMLongBench-Doc overall accuracy from 71.28% to 68.62%.
DocMemo Evidence Recall increased from 28.32% in retrieval-reasoning iteration 1 to 69.56% in iteration 3.
DocMemo All-Hit Rate increased from 12.90% in retrieval-reasoning iteration 1 to 58.05% in iteration 3.
Cumulative MMLongBench-Doc accuracy increased from 60.6% after iteration 1 to 65.5% after iteration 2 and 69.0% after iteration 3.
DocMemo used an average of 1.24 retrieval-reasoning iterations per question compared with a fixed 3.00 for SimpleDoc, corresponding to 0.41x relative computation cost and 2.40x relative efficiency.
In the iteration-efficiency comparison, DocMemo accuracy was 71.3% versus 60.6% for SimpleDoc on MMLongBench-Doc.
The default increasing lambda schedule [0.0,0.3,0.6,0.6] achieved 71.28% overall MMLongBench accuracy, compared with 69.04% for the reverse schedule [0.6,0.6,0.3,0.0].

On LongDocURL, full DocMemo achieved 81.2% mean accuracy (reported uncertainty ±0.3), versus 79.2% without Bayesian updating, 79.4% without all memory, and 80.8% without adaptive-granularity evidence access.

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: MMLongBench overall accuracy was 71.3% for full multimodal DocMemo, 58.6% for OCR-only, 69.3% for vision-only, and 69.9% without fine-grained visual crops.
The paper provides a public code repository at https://github.com/Harrygof/DocMemo.

The authors conclude that structured memory with dynamic probabilistic page-belief updating improves long-document visual question answering over static and iterative baselines, with adaptive-granularity access improving fine-grained evidence reading.

extraction_limitations: The paper reports benchmark and ablation results but does not provide an explicit standalone limitations section; no limitation atom was created from model appraisal.
No funding disclosure or conflict-of-interest statement was identified in the paper text inspected; none was fabricated.
Reported ± values for Table 12 are preserved as source-reported uncertainty without inferring an interval type or number of repeated evaluation runs.

Some benchmark baseline values are reported as taken from official leaderboards or prior papers; atoms here represent claims/results as reported by this preprint, not independent re-verification of those external sources.
